name: MMStar
description: An elite vision-indispensable multi-modal benchmark comprising 1,500 samples meticulously selected by humans to evaluate large vision-language models' multi-modal capacities across 6 core capabilities and 18 detailed axes, with carefully balanced and purified samples designed to ensure visual dependency and minimal data leakage.
creator: Zehui Chen, Haodong Duan, Jiaqi Wang, Yu Qiao, Dahua Lin, Feng Zhao, Lin Chen, Jinsong Li, Xiaoyi Dong, Pan Zhang, Yuhang Zang
citeAs: Zehui Chen, Haodong Duan, Jiaqi Wang, Yu Qiao, Dahua Lin, Feng Zhao, Lin Chen, Jinsong Li, Xiaoyi Dong, Pan Zhang, Yuhang Zang. Are We on the Right Way for Evaluating Large Vision-Language Models? arXiv:2403.20330v2, 2024.
rai:dataCollection: Samples are first roughly selected from current benchmarks with an automated pipeline, then strict manual review and selection are applied to curate 1,500 high-quality multimodal evaluation samples. The source benchmarks are SEED, AI2D, ScienceQA, MMBench, MathVista, and MMMU. The curation criteria are visual dependency, minimal data leakage, and requiring advanced multi-modal capabilities. After coarse filtering with LLM inspectors, three experts manually reviewed samples to ensure answers depend on visual content, cover comprehensive capability dimensions, and mostly require advanced multi-modal abilities. Samples were also grouped by difficulty using hit counts from 16 LVLMs into easy, moderate, hard, and tough categories.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Experiments
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The benchmark is constructed from six existing multi-modal benchmarks: SEED, AI2D, ScienceQA, MMBench, MathVista, and MMMU. The initial sample pool contained 22,401 samples, reduced to 11,607 candidate samples after coarse filtering, and finally 1,500 samples after manual review.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors developed an automated pipeline to preliminarily filter out samples that do not meet the criteria of visual dependency and minimal data leakage. They evaluated the sample pool with two closed-source LLMs and six open-source LLMs serving as inspectors, documented hit frequency for each sample, and retained only samples with hit counts of two or fewer. They also transformed some samples from uni-modal to multi-modal formats to prevent LLMs from recalling correct answers. Coarsely filtered samples were then split into four difficulty categories based on hit counts of 16 LVLMs before final manual curation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Open-source LLM inspectors were applied with a 2-shot in-context inference strategy to minimize response refusals and ensure consistency in answer formatting during filtering. For evaluation, all questions were ensured to be converted into a multiple-choice format, and heuristic matching rules were developed to calculate accuracy.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three experts conducted manual review of coarsely filtered samples to ensure each sample's answer should be based on understanding visual content, selected samples cover a comprehensive range of capability assessment dimensions, and most samples require advanced multi-modal abilities for resolution. The benchmark is organized into 6 core capabilities and 18 detailed axes.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To expedite manual selection of samples with varying difficulty levels, the authors tallied the hit counts of all 16 LVLMs on the coarsely filtered samples and split them into four difficulty categories: easy (12-16), moderate (8-11), hard (4-7), and tough (0-3).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Two closed-source LLMs (GPT4-Turbo and GeminiPro) and six open-source LLMs sizing 20B or larger were used as inspectors; 16 leading LVLMs were used to gauge sample difficulty.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: In the future, the authors plan to expand MMStar into a larger, online test set and explore dynamic evaluation methods to maintain sample visual dependency and reduce accidental data leakage into LLMs' and LVLMs' training corpora.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that inappropriate questions and data leakage can lead to misjudgments of actual multi-modal performance gains and potentially misguide the study of LVLMs. It emphasizes that transparent and equitable evaluation requires accounting for and mitigating leakage so models are evaluated on true ability to integrate and interpret multi-modal data rather than memorization.
rai:dataBiases: The paper identifies two benchmark biases/issues in existing evaluations: many samples lack visual dependency and can be answered from text alone or world knowledge, and unintentional data leakage exists in LLM and LVLM training. For MMStar specifically, the authors report that LLM performance is almost indistinguishable from random choice, validating significant visual dependency and minimal data leakage from LLMs.
rai:dataLimitations: Even the best model scores under 60 on average on MMStar, and the authors note particularly challenging dimensions including fine-grained perception, logical reasoning, science and technology, and mathematics. The paper also notes that existing benchmarks can suffer from visual-unnecessary samples and data leakage, which motivated MMStar. Future work is planned to expand MMStar into a larger online test set and maintain visual dependency while reducing accidental leakage.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models' multi-modal capabilities. It is used for evaluation/testing of LVLMs, including assessment with accuracy and the proposed multi-modal gain (MG) and multi-modal leakage (ML) metrics. The benchmark is designed to provide a fair and comprehensive arena for comparing existing LVLMs.
